  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#A8.SS6.SSS1.Px6" title="In H.6.1 Case 1 (Shared projector): a common PSD operator governs cross-layer interference. ‣ H.6 Shared projector makes cross-layer interference constructive ‣ Appendix H Analysis: Why Shared Projectors Increase Cross-Layer Gradient Coherence ‣ ROCKET: Residual-Oriented Multi-Layer Alignment for Spatially-Aware Vision-Language-Action Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Proposition 2 (Shared projector cross terms decompose into a common PSD part plus deviation).</span></a></li>
</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsubsection"><a href="#A8.SS6.SSS2" title="In H.6 Shared projector makes cross-layer interference constructive ‣ Appendix H Analysis: Why Shared Projectors Increase Cross-Layer Gradient Coherence ‣ ROCKET: Residual-Oriented Multi-Layer Alignment for Spatially-Aware Vision-Language-Action Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">H.6.2 </span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Case 2 (Multiple independent projectors): lack of a uniform constructive lower bound.</span></span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_subsubsection">
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#A8.SS6.SSS2.Px1" title="In H.6.2 Case 2 (Multiple independent projectors): lack of a uniform constructive lower bound. ‣ H.6 Shared projector makes cross-layer interference constructive ‣ Appendix H Analysis: Why Shared Projectors Increase Cross-Layer Gradient Coherence ‣ ROCKET: Residual-Oriented Multi-Layer Alignment for Spatially-Aware Vision-Language-Action Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Consequence for gradient stability.</span></a></li>
</ol></li>
</ol></li>
</ol></li>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">ROCKET: Residual-Oriented Multi-Layer Alignment for Spatially-Aware Vision-Language-Action Models</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">

</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">

<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author"><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">

</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable instruction-following robotic manipulation, but they are typically pretrained on 2D data and lack 3D spatial understanding. An effective approach is representation alignment, where a strong vision foundation model is used to guide a 2D VLA model. However, existing methods usually apply supervision at only a single layer, failing to fully exploit the rich information distributed across depth; meanwhile, naïve multi-layer alignment can cause gradient interference.
We introduce <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">ROCKET</span>, a residual-oriented multi-layer representation alignment framework that formulates multi-layer alignment as aligning one residual stream to another. Concretely, <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">ROCKET</span> employs a shared projector to align multiple layers of the VLA backbone with multiple layers of a powerful 3D vision foundation model via a layer-invariant mapping, which reduces gradient conflicts. We provide both theoretical justification and empirical analyses showing that a shared projector is sufficient and outperforms prior designs, and further propose a Matryoshka-style sparse activation scheme for the shared projector to balance multiple alignment losses. Our experiments show that, combined with a training-free layer selection strategy, <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">ROCKET</span> requires <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">only about 4% of the compute budget while achieving 98.5% state-of-the-art success rate on LIBERO</span>. We further demonstrate the superior performance of <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">ROCKET</span> across LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin, as well as multiple VLA models. The code and model weights can be found at <a href="https://github.com/CASE-Lab-UMD/ROCKET-VLA" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/CASE-Lab-UMD/ROCKET-VLA</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Spatial Reasoning; Vision-Language-Action Model; Representation Alignment
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><sup id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">∗</span></sup> ghsun@umd.edu   <sup id="p1.1.2" class="ltx_sup"><span id="p1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">†</span></sup> angliece@umd.edu</p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Robotic manipulation requires models to integrate semantic intent with precise spatial reasoning about objects, contacts, and constraints in the physical world. Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong instruction-following by leveraging large vision-language backbones, yet these backbones are predominantly pretrained on 2D imagery and often fail to produce representations with stable 3D structure <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zitkovich et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. As a result, VLAs may succeed on familiar scenarios but generalize poorly when manipulation depends on accurate geometry, viewpoint changes, or fine-grained spatial relations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shridhar et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To bridge this gap, prior work has pursued three main strategies to equip VLAs with spatial reasoning: (1) augmenting inputs with explicit 3D signals such as depth maps or point clouds <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shridhar et al., 2023</a>)</cite>; (2) recovering 3D structure from 2D observations via depth estimation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ranftl et al., 2021</a>)</cite>; and (3) implicitly aligning intermediate VLA representations to spatial features produced by pretrained 3D foundation models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Compared with the first two approaches, which rely on additional sensors or external depth estimators, implicit alignment is typically more inference-efficient and easier to scale, making it a particularly practical direction for improving spatial grounding in VLAs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">representation alignment</span> for improving spatial reasoning, a common practice is to supervise a VLA model’s visual-token representations to match those of a strong 3D vision foundation model. Most existing methods apply alignment at a single layer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. However, prior work has found that performance is highly sensitive to the chosen layer, and the optimal layer often varies across tasks and data distributions (as shown in Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Representation Alignment for Spatial Supervision ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ ROCKET: Residual-Oriented Multi-Layer Alignment for Spatially-Aware Vision-Language-Action Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). Since it is difficult to predict which layer contains the most appropriate visual representations <em id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">a priori</em>, single-layer alignment typically relies on inefficient post-hoc search. Meanwhile, representations in deep residual networks evolve with depth and encode information at multiple levels <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Skean et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and prior feature distillation studies similarly suggest benefits from leveraging teacher signals across depths <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gong et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. A natural alternative is multi-layer alignment, which can exploit hierarchical spatial cues from shallow to deep layers. However, in the VLA setting, directly extending classic distillation by aligning multiple depths with <em id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">independent</em> projectors per layer often backfires: separate projectors tend to learn inconsistent mappings between representation spaces, leading to severe gradient interference and ultimately causing performance collapse.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To address gradient interference, we propose <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">ROCKET</span>, a stable and high-performance multi-layer alignment strategy that formulates multi-layer alignment as aligning one residual stream to another. From a residual-dynamics perspective, we attribute the failure of naive multi-projector designs to gradient conflicts, and show that using a shared projector promotes gradient coherence. Concretely, <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">ROCKET</span> learns a cross-layer shared mapping via a lightweight projector that aligns residual streams from multiple layers to a target residual stream. This shared alignment helps reduce gradient interference, enabling fast convergence while continuing to improve late-stage performance.
We further observe that, in multi-layer alignment, shallower layers converge more easily; to prevent shallow-layer alignment from dominating the shared projector, <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">ROCKET</span> introduces a Matryoshka-style <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kusupati et al., 2022</a>)</cite> sparse activation scheme in which deeper layers activate more projector parameters. Such a scheme balances alignment losses across depths, encouraging shallow layers to quickly capture common local cues while allowing deeper layers to further refine global information. We also analyze layer selection and show that a simple training-free rule yields stable gains. Experiments across multiple models and datasets demonstrate that <span id="S1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">ROCKET</span> improves spatial reasoning in VLA models and consistently outperforms the single-layer alignment paradigm. Our contributions are summarized as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">ROCKET</span>, a multi-layer alignment framework that injects 3D spatial reasoning into 2D-pretrained VLA models, featuring a layer-invariant shared projector to avoid gradient conflicts and a Matryoshka-style sparse activation scheme to balance alignment losses across depths.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We develop theoretical and empirical analyses that explain when and why prior multi-layer alignment fails due to gradient interference, and show that a single shared projector is both sufficient and consistently superior to layer-wise projectors.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">By leveraging complementary spatial cues across depths, <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">ROCKET</span> achieves state-of-the-art performance on LIBERO and generalizes across multiple datasets and VLA backbones.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">ROCKET</span> is compute-efficient and converges quickly, reaching state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance with <math id="S1.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>4% of the training compute required by prior SOTA methods, while remaining effective in data-limited regimes relevant to embodied settings.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Vision-Language-Action Models and Spatial Grounding</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">VLA models integrate visual perception and language understanding to generate embodied robot actions. Representative works include <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OpenVLA</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OpenVLA-OFT</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2025</a>)</cite> built upon Prismatic-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karamcheti et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, as well as <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PI0</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PI0.5</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al., 2025</a>)</cite> based on PaliGemma <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Beyer et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which primarily rely on 2D Vision-Language Models (VLMs). These models often lack geometric understanding of the 3D world. To address this, several works augment VLA models with 3D information, including point-cloud inputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bhat et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025</a>)</cite> or depth-aware encodings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Meanwhile, recent 3D foundation models such as <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">VGGT</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Depth Anything</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> provide strong spatial representations that can offer rich supervision signals for 2D vision backbones.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Representation Alignment for Spatial Supervision</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Representation alignment (feature distillation) is widely used to transfer spatial knowledge from pretrained teachers to VLM/VLA models. Most prior work aligns student visual-token features from one layer to a fixed teacher layer. For example, <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Spatial Forcing (SF)</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GLaD</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2025</a>)</cite> align <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">deep</em> vision representations to VGGT features; <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">REPA</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> aligns <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">shallow</em> diffusion-model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peebles and Xie, 2022</a>)</cite> representations to DINOv2-Large <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oquab et al., 2023</a>)</cite>; and <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3DRS</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> supervises the <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">final-layer</em> visual tokens using VGGT. Although effective, these methods typically supervise a single layer and do not fully exploit the representations across depth. Moreover, as shown in Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Representation Alignment for Spatial Supervision ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ ROCKET: Residual-Oriented Multi-Layer Alignment for Spatially-Aware Vision-Language-Action Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the choice of which layer to align is often inconsistent across methods and depends on post-hoc empirical results.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S2.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S2.T1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison of representation alignment methods for spatial supervision.
